## Summary

We aim to get your laptop talking to a flashed G431 ESC via the flight controller, with the angular sensor wired on SPI. Lots of soldering. We will not use a battery for now, but a cable to a power source instead.

![How the battery, ESC, encoder, motor and microcontroller connect. The XIAO nRF52840 shown here is the separate-microcontroller option for serial described below - note that TX and RX are crossed. SPI3 and UART pin assignments match the rework in @tbl-spi3 and *ST-Link serial*.](/Fig/xiao-esc-wiring-diagram.png){#fig-wiring width="6.5in"}

Work through the module with this diagram open: every step below either wires one of these links or configures it in firmware.

## Electronic Speed Controller

The **B-G431B-ESC1** is ST's reference three-phase motor driver: a complete ESC on one small board, sold as an evaluation kit. It contains: - **An STM32G431 microcontroller.** A 170 MHz Cortex-M4 with hardware floating point. Motor control recomputes the field orientation every control loop. This MCU is the reason we can. - **A three-phase inverter.** Six power MOSFETs drive the three motor phases. - **A detachable ST-Link programmer (the daughterboard).** The small daughter board is how we program the MCU over USB, and it also carries a serial port back to the laptop. When snapped-off, the MCU cannot be reprogramed without physically resoldering it.

It also brings out many input/outputs (for example**J8**), a CAN transceiver and a potentiometer input, none of which we use as intended. In this build J8 gets repurposed for serial, and the encoder arrives on SPI instead. Both of those reworks are below. The board is rated well above what the wing motor draws (40A), so current is not the constraint here. Get familiar with every component on the board, how six MOSFETs turn one DC rail into three rotating phases, what current it can actually deliver, and why the programmer is a separate snap-off board under [The G431 ESC board](/reference/g431-esc.qmd).

## Flight controller microcontroller

We will use a **Seeeduino XIAO nRF52840 Sense** to send commands to the ESC and record information from the ESC. Why?

- It is small and light. 21 × 17.5 mm and 2.4 g. On a robot that has to move, every gram saved matters.
- It has wireless communication out of the box. The nRF52840 is a Bluetooth Low Energy chip and a microcontroller. Once the robot is sealed in [Module 10](10-waterproofing.qmd) BLE becomes the only way commands to interact with the robot during operation, which is exactly how a run is retrieved in [Module 11](11-wet-testing.qmd).
- It has somewhere to put the data. 256 kB of RAM and 1 MB of flash on the chip itself are the two logging destinations used during wet testing. No SD card, no extra memory chip, nothing else to waterproof.
- Onboard IMU to log the attitude of the robot without additional components.
- It costs 20\$. In case a failure, it can be replaced.

It programs from the Arduino IDE like any other Arduino board, but we highly recommend using **Visual Studio Code + PlatformIO**. The reason for PlatformIO is that it handles multiple-file projects much better, allows git versioning and handles libraries better. It also provides a more performant editor.

![The Seeeduino XIAO nRF52840. **TX** and **RX** are the two pads at the bottom corners --- those are the ones to solder to, and they cross over to the ESC's RX and TX respectively. The board is 21 × 17.5 mm, which is why it can ride on the robot at all.](/Fig/xiao-nrf52840.jpg){#fig-xiao fig-align="center" width="55%"}

1.  Solder the Seeeduino and the ESC's **Serial1**: TX, RX and **GND** lines. For that, use the 6x30AWG wire ribbon, spliced (only need 4 lines). In Serial communication, TX and RX are **crossed**, each board's transmit line goes to the other's receive line, as drawn in the [wiring diagram](03-esc.qmd#fig-wiring) in Module 3. GND is not optional: without a shared reference the two boards have no agreed voltage for what counts as a high or low bit.

2.  Verify that you can command the LED of the seeeduino on and off first. This requires Visual Studio Code and the PlatformIO plugin installed. Leave the ESC unpowered for now.

3.  Load the barebone Arduino sketch onto the Seeeduino, modify it if needed, see [Software](/reference/software.qmd) for the repository.

4.  Load the default ESC code onto the ESC via its daughterboard (via micro-usb).

5.  Prepare the USB-C 15V power source. We are using a USB-C power delivery cable to power the robot on the bench. A PD supply does not simply hand over whatever voltage you want. It advertises a fixed menu, and the sink has to negotiate for one of them, which is why we use a PD trigger cable or board is needed to pin it at 15 V. @tbl-pd is the power available.

    | Voltage | Max current | Power | Notes                                      |
    |--------:|------------:|------:|:-------------------------------------------|
    |     5 V |         3 A |  15 W | Default on plug-in, before any negotiation |
    |     9 V |         3 A |  27 W |                                            |
    |    15 V |         3 A |  45 W | **What we use now**                        |
    |    20 V |         3 A |  60 W |                                            |
    |    20 V |         5 A | 100 W |                                            |

    : USB-C Power Delivery fixed-voltage supplies up to 100 W. A source only has to offer the voltages at or below its rating, so a 45 W charger gives 5/9/15 V but not 20 V. {#tbl-pd}

6.  Solder the 2 power connection to the ESC using 40 cm of 0.5 mm2 silicone cables and connect 15V from a power source. Do not try to run motor for now.

7.  Modify the sketch to turn the LED on the **ESC** on and off via commander instructions. We now have confirmed three things:

    a.  The Seeeduino can be flashed.
    b.  The Seeeduino can be reached over serial.
    c.  The ESC is flashed.
    d.  The Seeeduino talks with the ESC.

## Encoder (or Angular sensor)

### First, why does the motor need an encoder?

Field-Oriented Control works by holding the stator's magnetic field roughly 90° ahead of the rotor's magnets, which is the orientation that produces the most torque per amp. To place the field there, the controller has to know where the rotor is **right now**.

Ordinary drone ESCs infer this from back-EMF, i.e the voltage the spinning rotor induces in the phase that is not currently being driven (@eq-bemf in [Module 2](02-motor.qmd)). That voltage is proportional to speed, so as the motor slows the signal sinks into the noise and the estimate falls apart. This causes *loss of synchronisation at low speed* described in [Design notes](/reference/design-notes.qmd). The AS5047P removes the guess. It measures the field of the magnet bonded to the shaft end and reports the **absolute** angle - valid at standstill just as much as at 15 000 rpm, and correct immediately at power-on with no homing move.

### What SPI is, and why we run it at 10 MHz

We will use an AS5047P encoder. The AS5047P reports angle over SPI, a four-wire synchronous bus: the controller drives the clock (**SCLK**), data goes out on **MOSI** and comes back on **MISO**, and **CS** selects the chip. Transfer speed is limited only by how fast the two ends can shift bits. We use SPI because it offers **10 MHz** communication. The reason speed matters is that the angle has to be re-read every single control loop, and a stale angle is bad: the controller ends up placing the stator field where the rotor **was**, not where it is. That error shows up as wasted current and audible noise. The same 10 MHz clock is why the wiring has to stay short, see below.

### Wire it to the board

There is no SPI link exposed directly on the ESC board. The solution is to use the **SPI3 bus**, exposed through a few hardware modifications and matching software changes. @fig-wiring shows the four signals in context, including the MOSI tap on R14.

::: callout-warning
#### The micro-USB serial link is lost

Serial2, used by the daughterboard for serial communication will not work anymore as we are using those pins for SPI3 for the encoder instead. Flashing the ESC still works (programming runs over SWD, on different pins) but every command and every value read back now **has to** pass through serial1 (external TX/RX).
:::

The encoder needs power as well as the four bus signals - six wires in total. Replace the default cable and use the 6x30AWG wire ribbon instead. This is small work! Sit down, use a clean soldering iron, take your time and make sure you have lots of light.

Check the R14 connection under the microscope. Use a drop of glue to fix the cable onto the board

![The MOSI tap on **R14** under the microscope. The wire lands on the outward side of the resistor, and the bead of clear glue over the joint is to help with accidental pulls on the cable.](/Fig/R14connection.jpeg){#fig-r14 fig-align="center" width="25%"}

|               | SCLK | MISO | MOSI  | CS   | 5V  | GND |
|---------------|------|------|-------|------|-----|-----|
| **MCU GPIO**  | PB3  | PB4  | PB5   | PA15 | --- | --- |
| **G431B pin** | J3   | J3   | R14\* | J3   | J8  | J3  |

: SPI3 connections on the G431. \* This connection is on the outward side of the resistor. {#tbl-spi3}

::: callout-tip
## Keep the SPI cables under 8 cm

Cables between encoder and ESC need to be **less than 8 cm**. At 10 MHz longer runs start corrupting angle readings, and the symptom is a motor that behaves erratically rather than a sensor that obviously fails. Check the length that is needed. The cables also need to be the same length.
:::

## Mounting

1.  Install the Seeeduino in its 3D-printed bracket and into the robot
2.  Install the encoder in its 3D-printed bracket (the tail stiffener)
3.  All mounted to the bottom fuselage plate

![Assembled motor-esc](/Fig/ESC_assembly.jpg)

::: callout-warning
## Warning

The first times that you start spinning the motor, it is critical to do that on a **current-limited** power source (**max 1A**), so NOT the USB-C one. Things can go wrong very quickly and if the motor is shorted you only have a few seconds to unplug it.
:::
